USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with this week's Beijing talks in a firm but non-escalatory posture — keep the proposed $50B Section 301 tariff list and the ZTE entity action on the table as leverage, but avoid any new escalatory move while the delegation is at the table. Treat the talks as the venue to secure a concrete framework on intellectual-property/tech-transfer practices and purchases, and be prepared to demonstrate progress rather than walk away without an agreed path.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is moderate (~+0.2), not existential: as of May 3 no tariffs on Chinese goods are actually in force — the $50B Section 301 list of April 3 is still in public-comment and would not take effect until late May at the earliest (Politico) — and US fundamentals show no trade-driven drag (industrial production rising, UMich sentiment ~98, fed funds tightening to 1.70%, no recession signal). The US holds the initiative: it escalated (Section 232, Section 301 memorandum, ZTE denial order on 2018-04-16) and China has responded only in mirror-image fashion ($3B on 2018-04-02; proposed $50B on soybeans/autos/aircraft on 2018-04-04), signaling resolve but also a return to the table. The main risk is a spiral that would hit US agriculture (soybean retaliation) and tech supply chains, and inject volatility into still-rich markets — hence not a clear opportunity. Action stance is hold-to-negotiate (action_score 0.0, negotiate): escalating further ahead of the talks would harden Beijing's position and cost the leverage that makes the modest threat manageable, while rolling back now would forfeit the negotiating advantage the proposed tariffs provide. Engaging talks without new commitments is the appropriate next step.
key_factors: Section 301 $50B tariff list published 2018-04-03 but NOT implemented (comment period to late May)
US economic team en route to Beijing for talks (Mnuchin, Ross, Lighthizer, Kudlow, Navarro)
US economy strong: industrial production up, sentiment ~98, no GDP drag from dispute yet
China retaliated tit-for-tat ($3B Apr 2; proposed $50B on soybeans/autos Apr 4) but returned to table
ZTE denial order 2018-04-16 = non-tariff escalation kept in reserve as leverage

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Engage fully in the Beijing talks now underway (US delegation led by Mnuchin meeting Liu He on May 3-4) and pursue a negotiating track rather than further escalation. We should press hard for relief on the ZTE denial order and for the $50B Section 301 list not to take effect, offering limited, reversible concessions (auto-tariff reductions, increased US purchases) while holding Our core interest firm: no concessions on the 'Made in China 2025' technology program. Do not escalate retaliation at this moment, because a full trade war would hurt Our export-reliant economy and tech supply chains far more than the US, and the US has opened a channel to walk this back.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is genuinely high but not yet existential. The April 16 US denial order banning American components to ZTE is an acute firm-level hit to a flagship telecom/5G champion and threatens its very survival ('could put the company immediately into a coma' per ZTE's chairman; 25-40% of its components come from US suppliers) — squarely matching the +0.5 'firm-level targeting' anchor, and the April 3 $50B list is deliberately aimed at Our ICT, robotics, aerospace and advanced-machinery sectors (the 'Made in China 2025' industries). So I score threat at +0.55. But several constraints keep it below existential: the $50B tariffs are still only proposed (public comment open), the broader economy has not yet absorbed a tariff shock, and we retain real leverage — Our April 4 counter-list on soybeans/autos/aircraft targets politically sensitive US export sectors, and Our status as the world's largest chip buyer gives us supply-chain weight. The ZTE episode is also energizing a nationalist, state-backed push for semiconductor self-sufficiency under the National Integrated Circuits fund, which is an opportunity embedded in the threat. This is exactly the wrong moment to escalate: the US has signalled willingness to negotiate (Mnuchin traveling to Beijing this week, markets and the moderate faction wanting to keep the dispute from spiking), and Our asymmetric dependence on US chips/software means escalation (further retaliation, refusing to talk) would invite a broader entity-list expansion that could reach Huawei and others, which would be far more damaging. A posture of engaged negotiation — no new tariff escalation while the talks attempt to trade relief on ZTE and the tariff threat for limited, reversible concessions — is the disciplined play. Escalation would make an already-high threat worse; negotiation is how we defend Our core interests and minimize damage.
key_factors: US April 16 denial order bans ZTE from US components — acute firm-level targeting of a flagship 5G/telecom champion
April 3 US Section 301 list of ~$50B targets China's ICT/robotics/aerospace sectors (Made in China 2025 industries)
US delegation (Mnuchin/Ross/Lighthizer/Kudlow/Navarro) in Beijing for talks with Liu He May 3-4 — negotiation channel open
China holds leverage: $50B counter-list on US soybeans/autos/aircraft and status as top chip buyer
ZTE ban rallying nationalist, state-backed push for semiconductor self-sufficiency (National Integrated Circuits fund)
Tariffs proposed but not yet in force; economy has not yet absorbed the shock
China's asymmetric dependence on US chips/software means a full trade war hurts us more than the US
